voice: Would you build a road that takes zero minutes? Watch what happens.
Four thousand drivers. Two routes. The mint roads slow with traffic: drivers divided by a hundred, in minutes. The gray roads always take forty-five.
Traffic splits evenly. Two thousand drivers per route. Twenty minutes on the busy road, plus forty-five on the other. Sixty-five minutes each.
Add a free shortcut. With the original traffic, one driver could do the trip in about forty minutes. What happens when everyone can use it?
Even at full load, each busy road takes forty minutes, beating forty-five. Everyone chooses both busy roads. Forty plus zero plus forty: eighty.
Why not switch back? With everyone else on the shortcut, either old route now takes eighty-five. No driver can improve alone.
Close the shortcut. Traffic splits again. Back to sixty-five. That is Braess's paradox: individual shortcuts can create a collective slowdown.
